draft.title: Egypt's wars and treaties
card: Ancient Egypt fought wars to protect its borders and to control trade routes and resources. Two of its main rivals were Nubia, to the south, and the Hittites, to the north-east.
Egypt wanted Nubia's gold and its trade routes along the Nile. At times Egypt conquered parts of Nubia and ruled them.
The Hittites were a powerful kingdom in what is now Turkey. Egypt and the Hittites fought over land in the region between them, and the Battle of Kadesh was one of their biggest clashes.
After Kadesh, Ramesses II and the Hittite king signed a peace treaty, an agreement to end the fighting. It is one of the earliest peace treaties known.
draft.remember: Egypt fought for land, trade and resources, and ended its long struggle with the Hittites by treaty.

a.q: What did Ramesses II and the Hittite king do after the Battle of Kadesh?
opts: Signed a peace treaty to end the fighting
Joined forces to conquer Nubia
Agreed to divide Egypt between them
Began a new war to win more land
a.why: The two rulers signed a treaty, an agreement to end the fighting, which is one of the earliest known. Kadesh was a big clash, but it did not lead straight to more war.
a.clue: Think about what a treaty is.

b.q: Egyptian officials in a Nubian trading town report that gold and trade goods are moving north along the Nile. Why would Egypt want to control Nubia?
opts: To gain its gold and its trade routes
To make peace with the Hittites
To stop the Nile from flooding each year
To move the Egyptian capital to Turkey
b.why: Egypt wanted Nubia's gold and its trade routes along the Nile, so it conquered parts of it at times. The Hittites lived to the north-east, so Nubia had no link to a Hittite peace.
b.clue: Nubia lay to the south, along the river, and had gold.

a.best: Signed a peace treaty to end the fighting

b.best: To gain its gold and its trade routes

problems.detail: Why (a) says Kadesh 'did not lead straight to more war', but Egypt and the Hittites kept fighting for years after Kadesh (c. 1274 BCE). The treaty came about 15 years later (c. 1259 BCE), so the why is misleading.
The clue 'Think about what a treaty is' names the word 'treaty', which appears in only one option, so a student can pick the answer without knowing the idea.

The stem says gold and trade goods are moving north along the Nile, and the clue repeats that Nubia had gold. Together they hand over the answer 'gold and trade routes' without the student needing to recall the card.
The distractors are implausible and easy to rule out: moving the capital to Turkey, and stopping the Nile flooding. The question therefore tests little.

check.summary: The card is accurate, but Why (a) wrongly suggests there was no more war straight after Kadesh, when fighting went on for about 15 years before the treaty. Both questions give their answers away: the clue in (a) names 'treaty', and the stem and clue in (b) state the gold and trade, with weak distractors.

proposal.title: Egypt's wars and treaties
card: Ancient Egypt fought wars to protect its borders and to control trade routes and resources. Two of its main rivals were Nubia, to the south, and the Hittites, to the north-east.
Egypt wanted Nubia's gold and its trade routes along the Nile. At times Egypt conquered parts of Nubia and ruled them.
The Hittites were a powerful kingdom in what is now Turkey. Egypt and the Hittites fought over land between them, and one of their biggest clashes was the Battle of Kadesh, in what is now Syria.

Neither side clearly won at Kadesh, and fighting went on for years. About 15 years later, Ramesses II and the Hittite king signed a peace treaty, an agreement to end the fighting. It is one of the earliest peace treaties known.
proposal.remember: Egypt fought Nubia for gold and trade, and fought the Hittites until both sides agreed to make peace.

a.q: Which best describes how the conflict between Egypt and the Hittites ended?
opts: Years after Kadesh, the two kings agreed to make peace
Egypt conquered the Hittite kingdom at Kadesh
The Hittites conquered Egypt straight after Kadesh
Both kings agreed to stop fighting on the day of Kadesh
a.why: Kadesh had no clear winner and the fighting went on for years. About 15 years later, Ramesses II and the Hittite king signed one of the earliest known peace treaties. Peace did not come on the day of the battle, and neither side conquered the other.
a.clue: Did the battle itself settle the conflict?

b.q: A pharaoh sends an army south along the Nile. Which rival is he most likely fighting, and why?
opts: Nubia, to control its gold and trade routes
The Hittites, to control the land between them
The Hittites, to take their gold and trade routes
Nubia, to win the land around Kadesh
b.why: Nubia lay to the south, and Egypt wanted its gold and trade routes along the Nile. Fighting over the land between them is a real reason for war with the Hittites, but they lay to the north-east, not the south.
b.clue: Check where each rival lay compared with Egypt.

a.best: Years after Kadesh, the two kings agreed to make peace
